title: ‘South Park’: Cartman, Stan and Kyle Must Solve South America’s Beef Crisis in Halloween Week Episode
description: In the fourth episode of “South Park” Season 29, South America’s beef has surprisingly become a hot commodity — and Cartman, Stan, Kyle and Randy w
body:
In the fourth episode of “South Park” Season 29, South America’s beef has surprisingly become a hot commodity — and Cartman, Stan, Kyle and Randy won’t let their lunch-of-choice get taken away from the local mountain town without a fight.

	The episode, titled, fittingly, “Guinea Pig on a Stick,” opens with Cartman eager to get a sloppy joe for lunch at South America Elementary. But to his horror, he learns there’s a national beef crisis, so the government is taking it from South America, and he and the gang will have to eat different versions of the four-legged rodent instead. But the kids (and Randy, who remains shrunken) won’t stand for this, and set off to find a solution after reflecting on what Kenny (who got blown up by an e-bike in the first episode of Season 29) would have done: not stand for this. 
	

	They visit the local ranch, where they learn that the suddenly premier, in-demand South American beef is just “the same cows that have always been here.” But, as the ranch worker responds, “Now we have a much higher clientele, you know, and all the rich people in other states want a premium experience.” He’s referring to national clientele outside of South America — specifically the chain Ruth’s Chris Steak House — despite the fact that every person who indulges in the meat literally explodes with diarrhea.

	Those eating the beef don’t care, though, as it’s become a symbol of “who’s more patriotic,” explains Randy, with politicians wanting to prove they support local South American beef. Plus, in the end, another chain, Sizzler, swoops in and steals all the cows. With no beef left, Stan has an epiphany: “They said nobody even really cares about our cows… So then, this rancher could inject anything with lard and butter, and people would be just as obsessed with it. That’s it, dude. That’s it. We can have all our cows back.” Indeed, it works, as the episode ends back at Ruth’s Chris Steak House, where a waiter is serving diners their new “patriotic meals”: flame-seared guinea pig on a stick.
	

	This week’s episode was decidedly not a Halloween special, despite the show’s storied history of spooky holiday episodes and its airing just a few days earlier. Thus, it appears creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone are skipping the holiday altogether. And though last year’s episode, titled “The Woman in the Hat,” wasn’t advertised as a Halloween episode ahead of its air date, it did come two days later than normal, timed to fall on the spooky night of Oct. 31.

	So far, Season 29 has centered a range of much-talked-about topics, including e-bikes, data centers, billionaires and anti-vaxxeres. In the third episode, the crew found themselves stuck in Sephora’s “backroom,” a nod to the joke that tweens spend ages in the beauty store, and dove into the internet-era term aura battles (meaning lingo like “mogging,” “maxxing” and “mewing” were plentiful).

	With Season 29, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone are going full steam ahead with the “South America” name change, which was announced earlier this month ahead of the Season 29 premiere. The premiere — the first episode since taking on the name “South America” — hit 4.2 million viewers in three days, as previously reported by Variety, and even featured an updated theme song to ring in the name change (and a Donald Trump cameo).

title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Football Heroes Take to the Battlefield in Peter Berg’s Emptily Macho WWII Epic
description: No one familiar with the oeuvre of Peter Berg — the action merchant behind the Afghanistan war drama “Lone Survivor” and the improbably pumped-up b
body:
No one familiar with the oeuvre of Peter Berg — the action merchant behind the Afghanistan war drama “Lone Survivor” and the improbably pumped-up boardgame adaptation “Battleship” — should approach “The Mosquito Bowl” expecting great restraint or good taste. Ostensibly, Berg’s Netflix-backed combat epic is fighting the same fight as Terrence Malick’s “The Thin Red Line,” likewise charting the physical and psychological torment of American soldiers in Guadalcanal during the Pacific Theater of the Second World War. But they are two very different history lessons. There’s not a hint of Malick’s poetic anti-war melancholy in Berg’s brawny, cacophonous Semper Fi salute to American military brotherhood, which certainly doesn’t stray from standard war-is-hell sentiment — rarely, in fact, has war been depicted as more loudly ruinous — but positively revels in onscreen carnage, as if to underline the mettle of its Marine heroes.
	

	Not that said mettle is in any danger of going unnoticed. For the four men at the pretty hollow center of “The Mosquito Bowl” aren’t just soldiers but sportsmen — stars of the college football circuit who bring their strength and smarts from the field to the battlefield. And if that comparison sounds glib to you, then buckle up, because the film has plenty more: “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in the history of football,” says one character, a sentiment that sounds sort of rousing without making much sense. That goes for much of the script by Berg and Mark L. Smith, which is drawn from a popular 2022 historical novel by Buzz Bissinger — the journalist whose 1990 bestseller “Friday Night Lights” became the basis of Berg’s sturdy 2004 football drama and the more popular TV series spun off from it. 
	

	Berg and Bissinger are cousins; the screen adaptation of “The Mosquito Bowl” was likely a fait accompli all along. Yet while the book’s ennobling mixture of Greatest Generation portraiture and brutal evocation of the rigors of combat is perfectly tailored to the filmmaker’s interests, it also hands the screenwriters a bit of a structural red herring. The title refers to a football game that the principals were tasked with organizing on Guadalcanal; it was played on Christmas Eve 1944 between the 4th and 29th regiments of the 6th Marine Division, and featured a wealth of drafted football talents who had set aside their sporting careers to serve their country. Outwardly, the book and film both seek to imbue this event with the significance of the famed Christmas truce soccer matches between British and German forces in the no-man’s-land of the First World War.

	When push comes to shove, however, the game simply isn’t all that consequential. It’s skipped over surprisingly swiftly on the page, and despite much anticipatory buildup, the film, too, struggles to make a climactic set-piece of an event that has considerably less visceral impact than the various juddering, blood-on-the-lens battle scenes on either side of it. Nor does it work as a human interlude, because the human dimension of “The Mosquito Bowl” is so flimsy. Its four principals are colorless, interchangeable alpha males, uniformly stout of build and square of jaw; they’re granted mildly differing character attributes by the script, but even as the closing credits roll, you’d be hard pressed to remember who was who.

	John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), a graduate (and future football coach) of Brown University, is given the leading perspective — which is to say he occupies the framing scenes that have him visiting a college football field years after the war with a stoic, misty gaze, and reflecting vaguely on all that has been won and lost. We rewind to 1941, when the earnest young man’s budding future with the New York Giants is put on ice by a surge of patriotic duty in the wake of Pearl Harbor; the same goes for jocular Purdue grad Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson, appropriating his father Jack’s rakish perma-grin), soulfully withdrawn Wisconsin Badgers star Dave Schreiner (stage star Tom Francis, a Tony nominee for “Sunset Blvd.”), and fellow Wisconsin grad Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), whose personality lands somewhere between those last two — the writers having run out of all-American archetypes quite early on.
	

	Historical dates are lightly fudged to give the four men a shared soldierly narrative, and so they collectively endure the grueling trials of Parris Island basic training, horrible but familiar from many a military drama, before shipping out to the Pacific, where the shattering, deafening mayhem that awaits them is horrible but familiar from many a war movie. Knowing that he has nothing new to show us, Berg’s solution is to show us ever more of the same, ladling on the frank images of death and devastating injury with relentless rat-a-tat-tat sound design to the point that the film does attain a blunt sensory force. 

	The aesthetic, with DP Jacques Jouffret’s aggressively desaturated palette and nauseous POV shooting coupled with antsy, abrasive editing, is ripped from “Saving Private Ryan,” but cranked up to video game levels, with a grinding, guitar-heavy score by post-rock band Explosions in the Sky; the film’s technical proficiency so overwhelms its slender character-building that it begins to feel almost heartless.

	The actors, all talented, are given no scope to be any more than capable. There’s scant room for inner life here, nor for reflection on anything more specific than war’s general cruelty — though, needless to say, the enemy gets even shorter shrift. There’s a jingoistic undertow to “The Mosquito Bowl,” with its flag-waving celebration of football and Marine fortitude, that sits queasily with decontextualized shots of Japanese soldiers committing ritual seppuku or being summarily executed by American captors, or the main characters’ repeated gung-ho statements about “killing the Japanese.” The film strains to say something about the morally corrupting effects of warfare, but doesn’t challenge its heroic leads on the racist invective they parrot, or circle back to any regret they may feel deeper into their service. Trivial and shoehorned in as it seems, when the titular football game rolls along, you can practically feel the film’s sigh of relief: at last, a blessed few minutes of macho combat without consequences — or politics.

schema.headline: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Football Heroes Take to the Battlefield in Peter Berg’s Emptily Macho WWII Epic

title: Vishal Bhardwaj, Shaunak Sen-Mentored Co-Production Fund Picks Ladakh-Set ‘Kakthet’ as Winner (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Stenzin Tankyong’s debut feature “Kakthet” (Idiot), set in the remote high-altitude region of Ladakh, has been selected as the winner of the inaugu
body:
Stenzin Tankyong’s debut feature “Kakthet” (Idiot), set in the remote high-altitude region of Ladakh, has been selected as the winner of the inaugural INR40 lakh ($42,000) feature film co-production fund run by Humans of Cinema and Safarnaama Pictures. 

	The Ladakhi-language project was selected from nearly 400 entries after an extensive screening and evaluation process.

	The film follows the precarious future of a government school and the community around it – both dependent on one reluctant grade 10 student who has never passed an exam, and whose teachers must attempt the impossible: save the school by saving the one student determined not to be saved.
	

	Tankyong has spent eight years making films that bring Ladakh’s stories, landscapes and culture to international audiences. His short films “Sekool” (2019) and “Last Days of Summer” (2023) have screened at festivals including the International Film Festival Rotterdam, the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival and the Dharamshala International Film Festival.

	“Kakthet” is produced by Ritu Sarin and Rajesh Thanickan, alongside French co-producers La Belle Affaire Productions. A filmmaker and producer whose career spans more than 30 years, Sarin co-founded both White Crane Films and the Dharamshala International Film Festival. Thanickan’s credits include Neeraj Ghaywan’s “Homebound,” executive produced by Martin Scorsese and premiered at Cannes in 2025; “Santosh,” which premiered at Cannes in 2024; and “Our Share of Sand,” which premiered at the 2026 Venice International Film Festival’s International Critics’ Week, where it won the Audience Award.
	

	The project had already attracted international industry attention before the fund selection, winning the Co-Production Features Grant at WAVES Film Bazaar in 2025 and being chosen as one of 30 projects for the 2026 Asian Project Market, held alongside the Busan International Film Festival.

	The fund was launched by Humans of Cinema founder Harshit Bansal and Safarnaama Pictures founder Nazim Momin, a U.S.-based engineer and producer. Filmmakers Vishal Bhardwaj and Shaunak Sen are attached as mentors, with Sen also serving as executive producer of the winning project. The jury comprised actor Imran Khan, filmmaker Arati Kadav, “All That Breathes” producer Aman Mann and festival director Aseem Chhabra.

	“The past few months working on this fund have been both unbelievably challenging and incredibly rewarding. We were pleasantly surprised by the sheer number of brilliant projects we received from across the country, and we’re even more convinced how desperately initiatives like these are needed in South Asia right now. It was definitely a testing process, but we couldn’t be happier with the result. Stenzin is an exciting new filmmaker with a distinct voice, and we’re excited to be an ally in his journey of making his debut feature,” Bansal said.

	“Stories like ‘Kakthet’ remind us why it is important to create opportunities for voices that emerge from outside the mainstream. I’m glad to be associated with this initiative and look forward to seeing Stenzin Tankyong bring his vision to life,” Bhardwaj said.

	“The ‘Kakthet’ script mobilizes lightness, absurdity and humor to tell the story of a slow lamentation underwriting several lives in Ladakh. The story of Singay and the motley group of students and teachers always stays curious and sensitive, while never lapsing into judgement. I look forward to supporting the team in realising this project,” Sen said.

	“I want to congratulate the Humans of Cinema and Safarnaama team who have worked tirelessly to create this fund. I was amazed at the passion, rigour and love they’ve put in selecting the winner. I want to congratulate the winning film and above all, I want to applaud all the filmmakers who applied. So many stories represented fearlessness and fierceness, and I was really inspired by them,” Kadav said.
	

	“I’m delighted that ‘Kakthet’ has been selected for the inaugural HoC x Safarnaama Pictures Co-Production Fund. For independent filmmakers in India, finding support for stories rooted in our own regions, languages and lived experiences can be challenging. The fact that this support comes from within our own country makes this recognition especially meaningful for us. For a film in Ladakhi, grounded in the culture and realities of Ladakh, this support offers real encouragement to tell a story that might otherwise struggle to reach the screen and a wider audience. Initiatives like this create valuable opportunities for newer voices in independent cinema, bringing the diverse cultures and experiences of our country to wider audiences. I’m glad Kakthet (Idiot) is part of this first edition, and I thank HoC, Safarnaama Pictures, the jury and mentors for helping us take the film forward,” Tankyong said.

	The screenplay is in its fourth draft. In July 2026, the team completed a three-week recce across the Changthang region and Leh for location scouting, production planning and the capture of visual and sonic material for a proof-of-concept teaser. Principal cast, crew and shooting locations are now in place, with the team focused on securing additional financing and establishing co-production relationships across Asia, Australia and Europe.

schema.headline: Vishal Bhardwaj, Shaunak Sen-Mentored Co-Production Fund Picks Ladakh-Set ‘Kakthet’ as Winner (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Smile 3’ Sets David Bruckner to Direct While Franchise Creator Parker Finn Helms ‘Possession’ Remake (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Put on a happy face, because “Smile 3” is officially in the works.

	Paramount has hired David Bruckner to direct and Nick Antosca to write the scr
body:
Put on a happy face, because “Smile 3” is officially in the works.

	Paramount has hired David Bruckner to direct and Nick Antosca to write the screenplay. They’re taking over for Parker Finn, who created the series and will remain involved as a producer alongside Temple Hill. (Finn pitched the framework for the third installment.) Jonathan Fass will executive produce.

	Bruckner’s credits include the 2022 “Hellraiser” reboot, 2017’s psychological thriller “The Ritual” and 2020’s supernatural horror film “The Night House.” Bruckner is particularly in demand as of late: he’s currently writing and developing a reboot of the sci-fi horror classic, “The Blob,” for Warner Bros., as well as Universal’s adaptation of “The Caretaker,” starring Sydney Sweeney, plus he’s set to direct “Mice” for A24.
	

	Antosca is best known for creating Apple’s miniseries “Cape Fear” and co-creating Hulu’s “The Act,” as well as writing 2021’s “Antlers” and the most recent Colleen Hoover adaptation “Verity.”

	Plot details for the third “Smile” movie haven’t been revealed. The first film stars Sosie Bacon as a therapist who becomes haunted by hallucinations after witnessing a patient die. In the second, Naomi Scott plays a pop singer who begins to experience a series of disturbing events as she embarks on tour. Since each “Smile” movie has functioned as a standalone sequel, with a separate story and new stars, it’s unclear who will appear in the threequel.

	Finn wrote and directed 2022’s “Smile” and the 2024 sequel “Smile 2.” The original film — commissioned for streaming before pivoting to a theatrical release — became a sleeper hit, with $105 million domestically and $217 million globally. The follow-up wasn’t quite as big at the box office but became a commercial win, with $69 million domestically and $139 million globally against a modest $28 million budget. In total, the franchise has earned more than $350 million worldwide.
	

	Although Finn isn’t spearheading “Smile 3,” he’s still working closely with Paramount, having signed a first-look deal with the studio after the first “Smile” became a theatrical success. Finn is directing a remake of the 1981 supernatural thriller “Possession,” starring Callum Turner and Margaret Qualley and set for June 11, 2027.

schema.headline: ‘Smile 3’ Sets David Bruckner to Direct While Franchise Creator Parker Finn Helms ‘Possession’ Remake (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Lord of the Rings,’ ‘Spider-Man’ Digital-Human Pioneer Remington Scott to Head Eros Imagination (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The Hollywood technologist who led Gollum’s motion capture on “The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers” and built the first digital humans made with
body:
The Hollywood technologist who led Gollum’s motion capture on “The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers” and built the first digital humans made with Light Stage technology for “Spider-Man 2” will run Eros Imagination, a new creative technology and experiences business set up by Eros Innovation.

	Eros Innovation, an AI company founded by the Lulla family that draws on the film, music and IP library of Eros Media World, announced Remington Scott’s appointment as head of the unit in London. Scott will oversee creative production, the development of specialist talent and international partnerships.
	

	The new outfit will mix human artists with visual effects, AI, digital-human tools, real-time production and games. Beyond serving Eros’ own businesses, it will go after deals with outside studios, streamers, filmmakers, game developers, musicians, estates and rights holders. It will work next to Eros Brahmand, the group’s film and content studio, and supply technology and production support for films, series, franchises and live immersive shows. Planned services run from AI-assisted filmmaking and post-production to immersive concerts, virtual production and playable game characters.

	One of its first projects centers on Mohammed Rafi, the celebrated Indian playback singer. Eros has a signed deal with Rafi’s family, and the plan is an immersive music experience that combines an authorized digital performance with cinematic storytelling, high-end visuals and audience interaction. The project depends on rights and creative approvals. Eros said it is meant to introduce Rafi’s music to younger audiences. It will also give the unit digital-human and production workflows that it could reuse with other authorized artists and properties.
	

	The unit will use Eros Innovation’s in-house Large Cultural Model (LCM) family, multimodal AI that covers language, images, video, voice and music. Eros built the models on its rights-controlled catalog, using about 1.5 trillion rights-cleared cultural tokens. Eros Imagination will team with the company’s India-based AI researchers and engineers to link the models with performance capture and real-time rendering, with humans leading the creative work. A system called Nexus will help choose the AI models and tools for each job, weighing quality, creative control, rights and cost. Eros said filmmakers and artists keep creative control.

	The unit will also draw on the AI-powered Creator Studio work Eros Innovation has done with U.K. government bodies and the British creative tech sector.

	Eros wants characters, artists and properties made for a film or live show to move into games, interactive stories, social content and new commercial formats where the rights allow it. The unit is also set to build digital identity systems that let artists and estates store, authorize and license digital versions of their faces, voices and performances. The company named consent, authenticity, provenance and IP protection as core principles.

	Ridhima Lulla, co-founder and co-president of Eros Innovation, said Eros Brahmand is where the company develops and produces stories, while the new unit “will help build the creative technologies and experiences that allow those stories, characters and artists to move beyond the traditional boundaries of film, music and entertainment. We are not simply bringing together a production team and third-party AI tools; we are building on Eros’s own Large Cultural Models, multimodal intelligence and extensive cultural IP. Remington brings an exceptional combination of filmmaking experience, technical expertise and creative vision, and our Mohammed Rafi partnership provides a meaningful starting point.”

	Scott has worked for more than 30 years across film, games and immersive entertainment. He was motion capture director on “Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within” and oversaw digital humans for “Superman Returns,” “Beowulf” and “Watchmen.” “Spider-Man 2” won the Academy Award for visual effects. On the games side, he has worked on “Call of Duty,” “Assassin’s Creed,” “Spider-Man” and “Just Cause.”
	

	He also worked on two Emmy-nominated immersive productions: the Notorious B.I.G. virtual concert “Sky’s the Limit” and a Fox Sports tribute to coach Jimmy Johnson for Super Bowl LIX. His other credits include a Madison Beer virtual concert that won awards and Netflix’s “Altered Carbon” AR experience, which won a Lumiere Award. TheWrap put him on its 2022 Innovators List.

	“Artificial intelligence, digital humans, real-time production and immersive technologies are giving filmmakers and creators tools that can fundamentally expand what is possible,” Scott said. “What excites me about Eros Imagination is combining these capabilities with Eros’s filmmaking heritage, extensive intellectual property and cultural intelligence. The Mohammed Rafi experience offers an opportunity to demonstrate how technology can celebrate a legendary artist while preserving the authenticity and emotional connection that made his work timeless.”

	Eros said more partnerships and projects for the unit will be unveiled later.

schema.headline: ‘Lord of the Rings,’ ‘Spider-Man’ Digital-Human Pioneer Remington Scott to Head Eros Imagination (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Emmy Award-Winning Actor, Comedian, Producer and Writer JB Smoove to Keynote at Variety’s Business Managers Breakfast
description: Variety will host its annual Business Managers Breakfast, presented by City National Bank, in Los Angeles on Nov. 12. The breakfast will bring toge
body:
Variety will host its annual Business Managers Breakfast, presented by City National Bank, in Los Angeles on Nov. 12. The breakfast will bring together those featured in Variety’s Business Managers Elite issue to celebrate the achievements of top entertainment business managers over the past year.

	JB Smoove – Emmy Award-winning actor, comedian, producer and writer (“Curb Your Enthusiasm,” “Saturday Night Live”) – will participate in a keynote conversation about his vision for modern storytelling spanning TV, film, branded entertainment and more. In addition to his on-screen work, Smoove founded Alternate Side Productions and First Darrin, a creative agency that collaborates with brands to develop campaigns, shorts, and other advertising-style content from a distinctly comedic, creative perspective.
	

	Media Cartographer Evan Shapiro will speak with Variety co-editor-in-chief Cynthia Littleton about his unique take on how the exploding creator economy is impacting the entertainment industry. He is a Webby Award-winning creator and an Emmy and Peabody Award-winning producer.

	Arnie Herrmann will be honored with the Variety Business Managers Elite Award in recognition of his exemplary career and contributions to our community. He currently supports such philanthropic organizations as Jenna’s Rainbow Foundation, Irving Penn Foundation and has served for many years on the board of MusiCares

	Hermann will be presented with the award by Award-Winning Actress Candice Bergen.

	“City National Bank has spent decades working alongside the entertainment industry’s top business managers, and we’ve seen firsthand the difference a great advisor can make,” said JaHan Wang, head of Entertainment & Sports Banking. “We’re honored to return as presenting sponsor of Variety’s Business Managers Elite breakfast to celebrate the people who help talent build careers that last.”
	

	“Business managers are a vital part of the entertainment ecosystem and we are very pleased to again partner with City National Bank for this event,” said Dea Lawrence, co-president and publisher of Variety. “We also congratulate Arnie Herrmann on receiving the Business Manager of the Year award.”

	City National Bank is the presenting partner of this year’s Business Managers Breakfast. Citrin Cooperman, Content Partners, Venable LLP, and Willkie are the supporting partners of the event.

schema.headline: Emmy Award-Winning Actor, Comedian, Producer and Writer JB Smoove to Keynote at Variety’s Business Managers Breakfast

title: Alexander Payne Hit With Copyright Suit Over ‘The Holdovers’ Script
description: A screenwriter sued Alexander Payne on Wednesday, alleging that the script for “The Holdovers” was based on his unproduced screenplay set at a chil
body:
A screenwriter sued Alexander Payne on Wednesday, alleging that the script for “The Holdovers” was based on his unproduced screenplay set at a children’s hospital.

	The screenwriter, Simon Stephenson, took his allegations to the Writers Guild of America in 2024, but was advised that the union could not adjudicate the issue and was referred to a lawyer. Payne later denied the allegations at the Sarajevo Film Festival, saying the claim was “the stupidest thing in the world.”
	

	In addition to Payne, the lawsuit names as defendants “Holdovers” screenwriter David Hemingson, producer Mark Johnson, Miramax, Focus Features, and other corporate entities. 

	The suit contends that there are 46 “matched incidents” in the plots of the two scripts. As described in the complaint, Stephenson’s script, “Frisco,” tells the story of a dispirited doctor at the hospital who is stuck looking after a precocious teenage patient. The two develop a friendship on a trip to San Francisco, culminating in the doctor’s decision to quit his job and set off on a cross-country trek.

	The lawsuit argues that the similarities with “The Holdovers” are more than mere coincidence, and that the structure and incidents of “Frisco” “were meticulously transposed into ‘The Holdovers,’ with surface cosmetic details changed.”

	“Screenplays are often called the blueprint for a film,” the lawsuit states. “The Defendants built their film using ‘Frisco’ as their blueprint.”

	Stephenson is an experienced screenwriter, with credits on “Paddington 2,” “Luca” and “The Electrical Life of Louis Wain.” He wrote “Frisco” in 2012-13, drawing on his experiences as a pediatrician, and the script was ranked third on the Black List — the list of the best unproduced screenplays in Hollywood.
	

	According to Stephenson, his agents sought to interest Payne in making the film, and got him to read it in 2013 and again in 2019. But he passed, the lawsuit states, with his producing partner telling Stephenson’s agent that “Payne did like it but was not interested in prod or directing it.”

	The suit alleges that elements of the “Frisco” script made their way into drafts of “The Holdovers” via Payne’s input to Hemingson.

schema.headline: Alexander Payne Hit With Copyright Suit Over ‘The Holdovers’ Script

title: ‘Pixels and Pencils’ Panelists Talk the Dangers of AI, Demanding Animation Processes and the Importance of Human Creativity
description: As artificial intelligence continues to advance, animators are increasingly facing questions about the future of their craft and the role of human
body:
As artificial intelligence continues to advance, animators are increasingly facing questions about the future of their craft and the role of human creativity in filmmaking. But the majority are not interested in letting AI into their art of storytelling.

	At Variety‘s “Pixels and Pencils” panel in Savannah, Georgia on Monday, leading filmmakers discussed the process of bringing animated stories to life and why technology can’t replace the work behind them. Six panelists joined Variety‘s Clayton Davis for the discussion, which was moderated in partnership with SCAD Savannah Film Festival. They included Brad Bird for Netflix’s “Ray Gunn”; Daniel Chong for Pixar’s “Hoppers”; Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado for DreamWorks Animation’s “Forgotten Island”; Travis Knight for Laika’s “Wildwood”; and Leah Nelson for Independent Film Company’s “Tangles.”
	

	Meg Weichman, the artistic manager of SCAD’s Theatres and Festivals, introduced this year’s panel, which she described as a celebration of the “imagination, artistry and collaboration that brings extraordinary animated stories to life.”

	But to make something “extraordinary” requires significant effort, which is part of what makes the process “magical,” Chong said.

	“Every set, every character, every piece of cloth, every piece of hair, every moment of atmosphere, all of that is created and made from ground zero. There’s no camera you can point at,” Chong told the audience. “It’s just completely fabricated and made and created, and that’s a pretty amazing thing, because that’s one of the reasons why I think these movies take so long, is because they have to create their own world.”
	

	Creating an animated film typically takes well over a year — and sometimes much, more more. From the first idea to its big-screen release, Bird’s “Ray Gunn” took roughly 30 years to finalize, though he wasn’t consistently working on the film throughout that period.



	

					“Ray Gunn” is voiced by Sam Rockwell and Scarlett Johansson.
									‘Ray Gunn’ ©2026 Skydance Animation
	



	But Bird was willing to put in the work, saying that a good story “has to come from life. You can’t create the illusion of life without having one, and that’s what we are in charge of — making the illusion of life and bringing people to something new.”

	“Wildwood” also required an extensive production process, especially considering it used stop-motion  animation. The film used 2,800 shots, a process Knight described as a “pain.”

	“Stop motion is progressive. You start on frame one and you work your way all the way through in slow motion until you have a performance,” he said. “There is something extraordinarily magical about being a part of that.”

	Despite the time and effort needed, the filmmakers said the process is what makes work meaningful. Chong added, “When you see people taunting that, ‘Oh, I can make this with the click of a button,’ or, ‘I can do this with these shortcuts,’ I think we just have to have faith that these processes are the way they are, and they’re as hard as they are to make for a reason, because that’s what makes these movies great and that’s what makes them resonate with humans.”

	The panelists agreed that the humanity behind these films allows stories to resonate with audiences — something AI can’t replicate. But the industry’s future remains uncertain as technology advances and animators continue to adapt. Bird advised artists in the audience to keep learning the ins and outs of animation as the field evolves . 

	The filmmakers also discussed how different animation styles can shape of story. Deciding whether to use 2D animation, 3D animation, stop motion or even Claymation depends on the film’s narrative, Mercado said.

	“It really is the story that dictates the visual storytelling and drive of the characters,” he shared. “That’s how we were able to play with various styles of anime and manga that followed the character point of view in these sections of [‘Forgotten Island’].”
	



	

					“Forgotten Island”
									DreamWorks Animation
	



	Crawford added, “For ‘Forgotten Island,’ we’re like, ‘This is an exploration of memories and how we experience them’ and thinking we all reflect memories in different ways. To have the animation style switch up depending on who the teller of the memory is was just a really exciting opportunity.”

	The panelists also challenged the common misconceptions of working as an animator, which for “Tangles” director Nelson, included actually needing to be an animator.

	“What I had to do, because I’m not an animator, was do everything else to communicate the vision — anything I could think of to communicate to my team what I hoped for and what I wanted to fight for,” she said. “I used all the other tools I could think of. I did a lot of acting references. I filmed myself doing the actions if I couldn’t draw it.”

title: From Carlos Reygadas to Hamaguchi’s Cinematographer, Tokyo’s Nippon Cinema Now Directors on Unexpected Connections
description: A first-time director who messaged Oscar winner Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s cinematographer directly, and a former hunter whose film led Carlos Reygadas to
body:
A first-time director who messaged Oscar winner Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s cinematographer directly, and a former hunter whose film led Carlos Reygadas to float a collaboration, were among five Nippon Cinema Now filmmakers who shared the unexpected connections behind their work at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF).

	The “How We Make Films” panel at Tokyo Midtown Hibiya, moderated by TIFF programming director Ichiyama Shozo, brought together Ueda Shinichiro (“Earthlings in Love”), Saito Kisin (“Kefi”), Natori Satoshi (“Chihiro | Akemi”), Matsumura Shingo (“Between Us”) and Yaza Takenoshin (“Hinotama: Ball of Fire”) to discuss the making of their radically different features.
	

	As he introduced the participants, Ichiyama noted that although the selection typically focuses on newer directors in Japanese cinema, he was interested in bringing Ueda in because of the unique vertical format of his latest film, “Earthlings in Love.” Ueda explained that the film was an adaptation of sorts, born from a 30-episode microdrama series designed for social media, hence the vertical aspect ratio. Its budget, though, was “equivalent to a regular independent film,” he said. That already sets it apart from most microdramas, which are typically very low-budget. “I’m from the theatrical film world, so we were making it as if it were a film to start with […] so it became appropriate for a theatrical release,” Ueda said.

	Ichiyama then introduced “Kefi,” a debut feature by young cinematographer Saito, which he described as “a very unique, strange film,” one where “you never know what’s happening, but at the end, it all comes together.” Asked how such a film came about, Saito said he had met a producer in charge of production and movie advertising, who found a sponsor for the project. “And so the sponsor had a theme for us, and based on that theme, we were going to make a film, and I agreed to it. But as we continued our discussion, the sponsor said that we could make it as we like. So it turned out to be a very strange film,” Saito said.
	

	The original theme, he said, was “maternal love, being a mother.” The finished film instead follows three sisters after they receive the news of their father’s passing. “They kind of left it to us, so I kind of just added my preferences,” Saito said.

	Moving on to “Chihiro | Akemi,” Natori spoke about a key location in the film, a house in eastern Hokkaido.

	“I wanted to shoot a film that is basically about the distance between the woods and the house, just going back and forth from the house. I myself used to be a hunter, and with the experiences from hunting, I came up with all these ideas, and I tried to put them in this film. You go out hunting, you look for prey, and then you hunt, and then you eat the meat. And you continue this over and over again,” Natori said. “And I kind of compared that life and the life that I have in Tokyo.”

	Natori, who used to work as a director at an advertising company, said that in the Hokkaido wilderness, those social roles were stripped away. “I really felt like my personality changed, and I was really interested in that shift, as if there was another person inside me. I fully felt this uncanny feeling of somebody else emerging from inside me, and I felt like this would be a really terrifying idea.” Nawata Canon, an actor and producer on the film, also incorporated her own experience of giving birth into it, Natori said.

	Discussing his influences, Natori cited Andrei Tarkovsky’s “Nostalghia,” calling it “foundational” because it taught him that “the plot is secondary.” To him, the texture of a film matters more, and color and style are equivalent to story.

	Natori also spoke about the film’s festival run, including the Split Film Festival in Croatia, where it won the Grand Prix in the feature film competition. That led to a meeting with Mexican director Carlos Reygadas, who was on the jury. “He came up to me and he said, ‘Your film is crazy. What’s going on here?’ So he personally talked to me and wanted to collaborate with me. So for the next one, potentially it’s going to be a Japan-Mexico collaboration,” Natori said.

	A common theme of the panel was the freedom to make the kind of film each director wanted. Speaking about “Between Us,” Matsumura said that “it was very much free in terms of what I could do with the concepts” in a film that “focused on theater and how the theater and reality overlap.”
	

	The conversation turned to taking a chance on approaching collaborators, with Yaza describing how he came to work with cinematographer Kitagawa Yoshio, known for his work with Hamaguchi.

	“I had never done a feature-length film or anything that required a budget, so I didn’t really know how much it would cost or what the budget would look like,” Yaza said. “But then I messaged [Kitagawa] directly. He has also done many low-budget films, and so I was curious.”

	He never imagined, he said, that “the cinematographer for Hamaguchi’s film would be able to join my project,” and assumed “there must be some kind of trick to make films with a low budget like Hamaguchi does.”

	Yaza asked Kitagawa about making films on a tight budget. That eventually led to a call in which the cinematographer offered to shoot the film and connected him with a producer, who began approaching financiers. “It was my first set because I’ve never been on a film set before,” Yaza said. “I was also the youngest person on set, and it was a very generous environment, [one] with an open mind, and we were able to enjoy ourselves until the end.”

	Natori’s thoughts on what matters most in feature filmmaking seemed to capture the idiosyncratic appeal of the Nippon Cinema Now selection as a whole. “I think it’s important for you to make a feature-length film that you will be satisfied by,” he said, “that you can only do because it’s your first time.”

title: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ First Reactions Call Prequel the ‘Rogue One’ of the Franchise and Praise Joseph Zada as Haymitch
description: “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” has officially premiered, and members of the film press are already calling the sixth installment a “per
body:
“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” has officially premiered, and members of the film press are already calling the sixth installment a “perfect adaptation” that breathes “new life” into the franchise. “Sunrise on the Reaping” is the second “Hunger Games” prequel movie following 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.”

	Film critic Griffin Schiller hailed the movie as the “Rogue One” and “Andor” of “The Hunger Games” franchise, adding: “It’s [a] sobering, yet powerful story of devastating loss and the necessary cost of rebellion for a sunrise we may never see. As a massive fan of the series and especially this book, I couldn’t have asked for a more perfect adaptation.”
	

	Filmhounds Magazine editor-in-chief and Tomatometer critic Gavin Spoors praised the film’s third act as “stellar,” writing that it “pulls the rug out underneath you.” “Anchored by terrific performances (Zada is a star), this emotional thriller nails the themes of the cost of revolution and how we all need to play our part,” he wrote on X. 

	Matt Neglia, Next Best Picture editor-in-chief, wrote that the film “features some of the best casting of the year” in his review. “Many of the actors breathe new life into familiar characters, making them their own, while preserving the qualities that made them so compelling in the first place,” he continued. “Glenn Close, with her horror-inducing face, is a scene-stealer as is Jesse Plemons embodying the spirit of the late great Philip Seymour Hoffman. Joseph Zada is beyond impressive in a highly demanding role that pushes him to the limit physically and emotionally, perfectly capturing the essence of Haymitch with all the sympathy, charm and bitterness Woody Harrelson brought to the role. I’m continually blown away by how Francis Lawrence continues to find more layers in this familiar structure thematically and stylistically as the production and costume design continue to be dazzling highlights. If this is to be the end of his time working on these movies, it’s a good way to go out as this latest installment brings the franchise full circle with the character that’s always been the beating heart at its center.” 
	

	“The rebellion is sparking with SUNRISE ON THE REAPING,” wrote fellow Next Best Picture editor Lauren LaMagna. “Francis Lawrence continues to breathe new life into this world. The unique production design doesn’t let familiar beats get too dull. Joseph Zada is heartbreakingly radiant as Haymitch. A star is born role.” 

	“One of the biggest highlights? Joseph Zada,” wrote Collider’s Perri Nemiroff. “I had high hopes for him after watching We Were Liars, but he had my jaw on the floor time and time again during Sunrise on the Reaping. His ability to capture Haymitch’s warmth and charm and then weave that into the rage and heartbreak the Hunger Games sparks is superb. SO much of this movie is on his shoulders, and he soars tackling every ounce of it. This is only the beginning for Zada.”

	She continued: “Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes bolstered my rewatches of the original films, and I have no doubt the same will be true of Sunrise on the Reaping. Sparking real change can take time and demand great sacrifice. This film franchise is better off for having added Haymitch’s.”

	Static Media writer Nina Starner also championed Zada’s casting, saying that it “couldn’t be better.” “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is a worthy addition to the franchise,” she wrote. “It looks and feels terrifyingly real, and it bridges the gap perfectly between the original stories and Ballad. A from me.”

	Based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest “Hunger Games” movie centers on a young Haymitch (Zada, taking over the role from Woody Harrelson) as he fights to survive while competing in the 50th Hunger Games. The cast also features Jesse Plemons as Plutarch, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman, Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket, Maya Hawke as Wiress and Kelvin Harrison Jr. as Beetee. New characters in the film franchise are played by the likes of Mckenna Grace, Glenn Close and Whitney Peak, among others.

	“Sunrise on the Reaping” takes place 24 years before the start of the first “Hunger Games” movie. Frances Lawrence, who has directed every “Hunger Games” movie except for the first installment (that was Gary Ross), returns to helm the latest prequel movie. 

	Much of the buzz surrounding “Sunrise on the Reaping” has been related to the franchise returns of Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Harrelson as Katniss, Peeta and Haymitch. Book readers know that Suzanne Collins’ novel ends with a flash-forward epilogue featuring the trio, so it appears the film adaptation is following suit.
	

	“It was unbelievable,” Lawrence said on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast about reprising Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional. Josh and I didn’t walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other. It was so beautiful.”

	“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” is set to open in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate. Check out first reactions to the movie below.

Lindsay Clancy's Lawyer
                          Fires Back At Ex-Husband's Attorney
                          ... 'Does Not Speak For Lindsay!!!'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 28, 2026
                            6:40 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Lindsay Clancy's attorney is firing back at her ex-husband's legal team ... flatly denying claims she plans to testify in a civil lawsuit against her medical providers. 
      
    
            In a statement released Wednesday, Lindsay's attorney, Kevin Reddington, blasted representations made by Patrick Clancy's attorney during a hearing in his ongoing wrongful death lawsuit against Lindsay's former mental health providers.
      
    
      
      STATEMENT OF 
KEVIN J. REDDINGTON, ESQ. https://t.co/u6QiVz1jiy
              @dnardo
          
  
    
            Reddington said, "Lindsay Clancy never told any of her healthcare providers that she harbored homicidal ideation toward her children."
      
    
            He also pushed back on claims Lindsay is prepared to take the stand in Patrick's civil case, saying she never indicated she intended to testify and no one representing her ever suggested otherwise.
      
    
            Reddington ended his statement with a pointed message ... "Mr. Clancy's counsel does not speak for Lindsay Clancy."
      
    
            The statement came after Patrick's attorney told a Massachusetts judge Wednesday he believes Lindsay will testify that she explicitly informed her medical providers she was experiencing homicidal thoughts and feared something terrible could happen to her children.
      
    
            The dispute unfolded during a hearing over a motion to dismiss Patrick's lawsuit against Lindsay's former medical providers, whom he accuses of mishandling her mental health treatment before the January 2023 deaths of their three kids -- Cora, Dawson, and Callan.
      
    
            As we reported ... Lindsay was charged with murdering the children before attempting suicide. Her defense argued she suffered from postpartum psychosis, but prosecutors disagreed. Her trial ended in a mistrial in September.
      
    
            Patrick has since divorced Lindsay, who filed her own medical malpractice lawsuit. A judge has yet to rule on Patrick's case, and Lindsay could face a retrial.
